subject: schumer

brief.inclusion: Senate Democratic leader since 2017 (majority leader 2021–2025), the first Jewish leader of either party in the Senate, who steered the Biden-era industrial and climate laws, organized the Senate's first bipartisan AI policy process, and now leads his party into the 2026 midterms under pressure from its left.

summary: New York's senior senator since 1999 and Senate Democratic leader since 2017, majority leader from 2021 to 2025 when the Senate passed the American Rescue Plan, the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act; he was the first Jewish Senate leader. He convened the Senate's AI Insight Forums and its 2024 AI roadmap, called in March 2024 for Israel to hold new elections, and in 2025 drew calls to step down from his own party's left after a March funding vote and the 43-day fall shutdown.

chapters.title: Brooklyn to Albany to Congress
chapters.dek: A career politician from law school onward.
chapters.body: Schumer was born in Midwood, Brooklyn, on November 23, 1950, and was valedictorian of James Madison High School in 1967. He graduated from Harvard College in 1971 and Harvard Law School in 1974, the year he was elected to the New York State Assembly [[wikipedia]]. After six years in Albany he won a House seat in 1980 and served nine terms representing parts of Brooklyn and Queens [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Senator and party fundraiser
chapters.dek: Beating D'Amato and running the Senate campaign committee.
chapters.body: In 1998 Schumer unseated Republican Sen. Al D'Amato and took office in January 1999, becoming New York's senior senator when Daniel Patrick Moynihan retired in 2001 [[wikipedia]]. As chairman of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee from 2005 to 2009 and was vice chair of the Democratic caucus from 2007 to 2017 [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Democratic leader and majority leader
chapters.dek: The Biden agenda, and the Senate's first serious look at AI.
chapters.body:
Schumer succeeded Harry Reid as Senate Democratic leader in 2017, the first Jewish leader of either party in the Senate, and became majority leader of a 50–50 chamber in January 2021 [[wikipedia]]. Over the next two years the Senate passed the American Rescue Plan, the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act [[wikipedia]].

He also made artificial intelligence a leadership project. With Senators Mike Rounds, Martin Heinrich and Todd Young he convened nine AI Insight Forums in 2023 with technology executives, researchers and advocates, and on May 15, 2024, the group released a bipartisan roadmap calling for at least $32 billion a year in non-defense AI research funding, meant as a foundation for committee legislation [[mayer-brown-ai-2024]].

chapters.title: "Shomer Yisroel"
chapters.dek: A call for new Israeli elections and a book on antisemitism.
chapters.body:
On March 14, 2024, Schumer, describing his role as "Shomer Yisroel — a guardian of the People of Israel," told the Senate that Benjamin Netanyahu had "lost his way" and that a new Israeli election was needed. "Israel cannot survive if it becomes a pariah," he said, while adding that Israelis should choose their own leaders and "we should let the chips fall where they may." Mitch McConnell called the speech grotesque, House Speaker Mike Johnson called it inappropriate, and Israel's ambassador called it counterproductive [[ap-israel-2024]].

That August he announced Antisemitism in America: A Warning, published by Grand Central in 2025. "Jewish Americans never thought it could happen here in America," he said. "Now, for the first time, they're worried it could" [[ji-book-2024]].

chapters.title: Leading the opposition, and his critics
chapters.dek: Two funding fights in 2025 and a final campaign for the majority.
chapters.body:
Back in the minority in 2025, Schumer surprised his party in March by voting to advance a Republican stopgap funding bill after signaling he would oppose it. He argued that a shutdown "would be 15 or 20 times worse" because "there's no off-ramp," and said he would not step down despite calls from progressives to do so [[hill-cr-2025]].

In the fall he led Democrats into the longest government shutdown in U.S. history over health-care funding. It ended in November when eight members of his caucus, led by Jeanne Shaheen, voted with Republicans; Schumer voted no. Rep. Ro Khanna and other House progressives, MoveOn and activist groups called on him to quit as leader, though no Democratic senator did [[wapo-shutdown-2025]].

In October 2026, at 75 and after 52 years in public office, he was campaigning for a Democratic Senate majority; Axios reported that he was "more than favored" to keep the leadership in a secret-ballot vote if Democrats won it [[politicalwire-2026]].
